S3.2. Unit conventions

All translation columns of the released CSVs are in meters and are converted to mil-
limeters before the position RMSE entry of the main-text summary table is computed
(Section S3.3). The translation columns of the orientation-experiment CSVs are not
used in the orientation analysis. Orientation CSVs report the measured rotation as
Rodrigues vectors in radians, and orientation error is computed from the geodesic
angular distance between the measured and reference rotations.


S3.3. Analysis steps

The fixed-camera entries of the main-text summary table, namely the frontal-cell
(θx = θy = 0) mean±SD orientation errors of the broad grid and the position RMSEs,
are obtained from the CSV files listed above by the following steps:

• the evaluation of the orientation error as the SO(3) geodesic distance between the
  measured and the robot-commanded relative orientation, computed from a fixed
  ideal reference orientation after removing a single constant camera-to-command
  frame offset estimated robustly across all poses: the offset is the rotation minimizing
  the mean SO(3) log-residual (the residual rotation angle) over all samples, refitted
  with samples whose residual exceeds 12° (pose flips) excluded from the fit (at most
  three passes) while all samples are retained in the reported error.
• the  reduction  of  the  position measurements  to a common  millimeter  scale
  (Section S3.2), followed by a global axis-sign resolution (sign of the command–
  measurement correlation per axis) and the removal of a single constant in-plane
  frame offset, fitted as a two-dimensional rigid Procrustes (Kabsch) alignment of all
  measured positions onto the commanded grid. The fit is made robust by excluding
  samples whose residual exceeds three times the current root-mean-square residual


                                    43  and refitting (at most three passes), while all samples are retained in the reported
   error, taken as the Euclidean residual to the commanded relative translation.

Sample standard deviation (ddof = 1) is used throughout. The cell-wise tables and
difference maps of Section S2.3 apply the same conventions to every commanded cell.
The closed-loop entries of the main-text summary table and Table S6 are the within-
run means over the common window defined in Section S5, which also specifies the
representative-run rule and the statistical tests.

The alignment parameters are fitted to the same samples on which the errors are eval-
uated. They therefore remove the global frame mismatch together with any constant
marker-specific bias. The resulting values do not measure absolute pose bias or held-
out calibration accuracy. Because one constant transform is shared by all commanded
cells, pose-dependent patterns across the grid remain in the errors. The 10 frames
at each cell are consecutive images of one held pose and quantify within-acquisition
variation, not variability across independent re-mountings. No frame-level significance
inference is used for the main fixed-camera claims.

For reference, two auxiliary quantities quoted in Section 4.2 of the main text are
obtained from the same position datasets: the mean within-cell standard deviation of
the measured positions is 0.02–0.03 mm for the three quARtet layouts and 0.15 mm
for Single, and the fitted constant in-plane frame offset includes an in-plane rotation of
approximately −3.1° in all four datasets. This agreement is compatible with a common
camera-to-robot frame mismatch but is not an independent validation, because each
offset is fitted to its evaluated dataset. The manufacturer’s ±0.03 mm repeatability
specification is translational and comparable to the smallest within-cell variations. No
external orientation-reference uncertainty was measured.

                                 -1 -                       A b s t r a c t

This thesis deals with the various aspects of obtaining a 3D map of a scene using
passive stereo vision. The ultimate goal of this research is solving the correspondence
problem. The correspondence problem is considered to be an ill-posed problem which
has to be constrained in order for it to become solvable. Various generic constraints are
discussed. The thesis is in favour of the edge matching first and surface reconstruction
second strategy. This view is supported  1by the success of the simple edgel-segment
based stereo matching algorithms. Edge detection is the only preprocessing necessary
for stereo matching. Based on Canny's edge detection scheme, a comparison of the
convolution of image with the first derivative of a Gaussian and the Gaussian followed
by the Sobel operators is made.

Two main issues that are addressed in the thesis are the accuracy and reliability of the
recovered 3D data. The problem of stereo camera calibration is investigated with
emphasis on the calibration accuracy. Empirical studies have been carried out in order
to find an “optimal” stereo camera configuration in which the effects of spatial
discretization errors in the stereo system can be reduced. An empirical model for
estimating the average triangulation error in a convergent stereo system is presented.

The correspondence problem is formulated in the framework of combinatorial
optimization. A deterministic algorithm as opposed to a stochastic algorithm is favoured
in the case of a well constrained stereo system. Two stereo matching algorithms are
presented. The Hit and Track Local Optimal Selection algorithm exploits the property of
disparity continuity along an edge segment. The Edgel-segment based matching by the
L-Deque Shortest Path algorithm is developed based on the analogy between edgel
matching along an edge segment and layered network optimization. A comparison of
these two algorithms is presented.

{"answer": "## Evidence relevant to the camera layout

**Yes—two calibrated, substantially separated views are preferable to one for an independent three-dimensional check of the PiPER fingertips.** A third view is valuable primarily for surviving occlusion and improving coverage; it does not automatically improve precision. The studies below do not establish a universally optimal camera distance or crossing angle, nor do their best reported errors directly predict accuracy on this table. In particular, distinguish *camera-measurement error* from *robot error measured using cameras* and from *target-registration error after fitting a reference frame*. (pqac-00000010, pqac-00000011, pqac-00000033)

<artifact id="artifact-00"/>

The closest direct robot-calibration example is Wang and colleagues’ binocular measurement of three ceramic spheres on an ABB six-axis arm. At approximately **0.5–1.0 m** camera-to-end-effector distance, the mean discrepancy between commanded and vision-measured movements fell from **0.7873 to 0.2604 mm** after kinematic calibration; the post-calibration maximum was **0.7107 mm**. These are discrepancies *relative to the camera system*, not an independently established 0.26-mm accuracy for its sphere localization, and the industrial arm and optics differ from PiPER and Camera Module 3 Wide. (pqac-00000024, pqac-00000026, pqac-00000032, pqac-00000033)

For a controlled camera-count comparison, Sideris and colleagues placed **five** Raspberry Pi global-shutter cameras around a **72-cm-diameter** fixture approximately **1 m above** the measurement volume and tracked ArUco-marked three-dimensional fiducials. Their cropped Table 1 shows improving target-registration performance overall from one to five views, particularly on a three-dimensional phantom, but an intermediate three-camera triangulation configuration was *worse* than some two-camera configurations on the planar grid. Their approximately **0.64-mm** five-camera grid figure is a median *individual point* error; the corresponding **0.7477-mm** value in Table 1 is a median of trial/configuration RMSEs. Neither should be read as demonstrated fingertip accuracy across PiPER’s entire workspace. (pqac-00000016, pqac-00000017, pqac-00000018, pqac-00000019, pqac-00000029, pqac-00000010, pqac-00000011)

## Why viewing angles matter

There are **two different angles** to optimize. First, the *angle between rays from different cameras to the fingertip* should be substantial: nearly coincident cameras provide little independent depth information. For a conventional parallel stereo pair, depth uncertainty scales approximately as **Z²σd/(fB)**, where *Z* is range, *f* focal length in pixels, *B* baseline, and *σd* disparity uncertainty. This is a geometric approximation, **not** a measured error for the proposed cameras. state.question: Setup: a tabletop 6-DOF robot arm (AgileX PiPER, about 0.63 m reach, fingertips reach about 0.76 m at table height) on a 1.29 x 1.36 m table against a wall. Current proposal: one camera about 1.2 m above the table looking straight down, one about 0.8 m from the arm base past the table end the arm faces at joint 1 = 0, about 0.42 m up and tilted 19 deg down, and a third low camera on the room-side table edge looking toward the wall. For checking or calibrating the kinematic accuracy of a low-cost serial robot arm with fixed external cameras and a fiducial (ArUco, AprilTag or ChArUco board, or a sphere) on the end effector, what camera distances, viewing angles and numbers of cameras have given the best end-effector position accuracy, what accuracies (mm) were achieved, and how does the viewing angle of a planar fiducial (frontal vs oblique) affect its pose and depth accuracy? Does the evidence favour two or more cameras at large angular separation over a single camera?

(sideris2026larkalowcost pages 3-4, wang2023separationandcalibration pages 10-12, sideris2026larkalowcost pages 8-9, sideris2026larkalowcost pages 4-5)

4. **Validate the measurement system separately from the kinematics.** Calibrate each camera’s intrinsics and wide-lens distortion at its final focus and resolution; estimate inter-camera extrinsics with a measured board seen across the three-dimensional working volume, and securely mount cameras independently of the moving arm. Establish the board/table/robot-base transform and marker-to-TCP offset; then compare visually triangulated positions against encoder-based forward kinematics at *held-out poses spanning height and reach*. Report repeatability, systematic error and worst-case error separately, including fingertip poses with partial occlusion. To claim that a detected few-millimetre discrepancy is true robot drift, verify camera/TCP accuracy against an **independent** measured target or metrology reference—not merely the same robot commands used for calibration. Static image capture reduces blur and timing concerns; for motion, synchronize observations. (sideris2026larkalowcost pages 5-7, sideris2026larkalowcost pages 12-13, wakiuchi2610quartetmarkera pages 12-18, maghami2024visionbasedtargetlocalization pages 14-17, sideris2026larkalowcost pages 4-5)

**Bottom line:** the evidence supports **at least two well-calibrated cameras with complementary, appreciably separated sightlines**, and preferably a third for this cluttered, moving tabletop. It does **not** show that three cameras must always outperform two, that exactly 90° is optimal, or that one wide, overhead monocular image can independently verify few-millimetre *3D* fingertip drift. A single close camera with a well-designed **3D fiducial** can nevertheless provide useful relative pose measurements; that is a different, more marker- and calibration-dependent claim than robust multiview triangulation. (sideris2026larkalowcost pages 12-13, sideris2026larkalowcost pages 13-14, wakiuchi2610quartetmarkera pages 18-22, wakiuchi2610quartetmarkera pages 10-12)
answer.raw_answer:
## Evidence relevant to the camera layout

**Yes—two calibrated, substantially separated views are preferable to one for an independent three-dimensional check of the PiPER fingertips.** A third view is valuable primarily for surviving occlusion and improving coverage; it does not automatically improve precision. The studies below do not establish a universally optimal camera distance or crossing angle, nor do their best reported errors directly predict accuracy on this table. In particular, distinguish *camera-measurement error* from *robot error measured using cameras* and from *target-registration error after fitting a reference frame*. (pqac-00000010, pqac-00000011, pqac-00000033)

| Study and geometry / marker | Evaluation metric and measured accuracy | Interpretation |
|---|---|---|
| **Wang et al. (2023)** — binocular camera; ABB IRB-1200; three 25.4 mm ceramic spheres; camera-to-end-effector distance approximately 0.5–1.0 m (pqac-00000024, pqac-00000032) | Across 40 commanded motions of 50–100 mm: mean discrepancy **0.7873 to 0.2604 mm** after kinematic calibration; maximum **1.998 to 0.7107 mm** (pqac-00000033) | Strong short-range stereo result, but the camera measurement defines the observed motion; this is **not independently verified vision-localization error**. |
| **Wakiuchi et al. (2026)** — one fixed camera at approximately 0.22 m; 35 mm planar AprilTag versus 35 mm non-coplanar four-tag fiducials (pqac-00000030) | At fixed frontal orientation over a translation grid: planar-tag positional RMSE **1.50 mm**; non-coplanar four-tag designs **0.17–0.20 mm** (pqac-00000014) | Demonstrates near-frontal planar-tag ill-conditioning, not absolute accuracy: the reference was robot-commanded motion, and a constant transform was fitted to the evaluated data (pqac-00000049). |
| **Sideris et al. (2026), LARK — planar grid** — five Raspberry Pi global-shutter cameras in a pentagon on a 0.72 m fixture, approximately 1 m above the target; 24 mm ArUco tags on a dodecahedron (pqac-00000019, pqac-00000054) | Adaptive-triangulation **target-registration RMSE median**: 2 cameras **0.9584 mm**, 3 **1.0000 mm**, 4 **0.9030 mm**, 5 **0.7477 mm**. With five cameras, the median individual point error was **0.64 mm** (pqac-00000010, pqac-00000011). | Five cameras achieved submillimetre grid performance, but improvement with camera count was not monotonic: configuration and ray geometry mattered. The 0.7477 and 0.64 mm values summarize different units—trial/configuration RMSEs and individual target-point errors, respectively. |
| **Sideris et al. (2026), LARK — head phantom** — same hardware under greater depth variation, oblique views, and partial occlusion | One-camera monocular target-registration RMSE median **2.7304 mm**; adaptive triangulation: 2 cameras **1.7163 mm**, 3 **1.6082 mm**, 4 **1.3957 mm**, 5 **1.2774 mm**. Five-camera median individual point error: **1.13 mm** (pqac-00000010, pqac-00000012). | Accuracy improved consistently from two to five triangulating views, but realistic geometry eliminated the grid’s submillimetre result. Laboratory grid accuracy therefore should not be treated as whole-workspace absolute accuracy. |


*Table: Compact comparison of robot and fiducial localization results, including camera geometry, measured accuracy, and validation limitations. Values based on different aggregation methods are explicitly distinguished.*

The closest direct robot-calibration example is Wang and colleagues’ binocular measurement of three ceramic spheres on an ABB six-axis arm. At approximately **0.5–1.0 m** camera-to-end-effector distance, the mean discrepancy between commanded and vision-measured movements fell from **0.7873 to 0.2604 mm** after kinematic calibration; the post-calibration maximum was **0.7107 mm**. These are discrepancies *relative to the camera system*, not an independently established 0.26-mm accuracy for its sphere localization, and the industrial arm and optics differ from PiPER and Camera Module 3 Wide. (pqac-00000024, pqac-00000026, pqac-00000032, pqac-00000033)

For a controlled camera-count comparison, Sideris and colleagues placed **five** Raspberry Pi global-shutter cameras around a **72-cm-diameter** fixture approximately **1 m above** the measurement volume and tracked ArUco-marked three-dimensional fiducials. Their cropped Table 1 shows improving target-registration performance overall from one to five views, particularly on a three-dimensional phantom, but an intermediate three-camera triangulation configuration was *worse* than some two-camera configurations on the planar grid. Their approximately **0.64-mm** five-camera grid figure is a median *individual point* error; the corresponding **0.7477-mm** value in Table 1 is a median of trial/configuration RMSEs. Neither should be read as demonstrated fingertip accuracy across PiPER’s entire workspace. (pqac-00000016, pqac-00000017, pqac-00000018, pqac-00000019, pqac-00000029, pqac-00000010, pqac-00000011)

## Why viewing angles matter

There are **two different angles** to optimize. First, the *angle between rays from different cameras to the fingertip* should be substantial: nearly coincident cameras provide little independent depth information. For a conventional parallel stereo pair, depth uncertainty scales approximately as **Z²σd/(fB)**, where *Z* is range, *f* focal length in pixels, *B* baseline, and *σd* disparity uncertainty. This is a geometric approximation, **not** a measured error for the proposed cameras. A roughly orthogonal overhead–side pairing near the working region can therefore be useful, provided **both cameras actually see the same identifiable feature**. A wide baseline that loses joint visibility or produces severe marker foreshortening is counterproductive; LARK’s non-monotonic subset results illustrate that qualification. (pqac-00000009, pqac-00000010, pqac-00000011, pqac-00000028)

Second, consider the angle **between each camera’s sightline and a planar marker’s normal**. A nearly face-on tag can have excellent apparent area yet weak perspective cues for its *tilt*, permitting competing near-mirror pose estimates; an extremely oblique tag loses projected area and detectable corners. In a particularly relevant **single fixed-camera**, approximately **220-mm-range** experiment, a 35-mm planar AprilTag gave **2.18° ± 0.80°** frontal orientation error, versus approximately **0.15–0.6°** across oblique cells with commanded tilts of **15–30°**. Its positional RMSE over translations made *while held frontally* was **1.50 mm**, compared with **0.17–0.20 mm** for non-coplanar four-tag markers occupying the same footprint. Those position figures combine coordinate directions, including commanded depth changes: the study does **not** establish a separate 1.50-mm depth error. Crucially, its reference was robot-commanded *relative* motion with an alignment fitted on the evaluated measurements—not external absolute ground truth. Moderate obliquity helps the planar tag’s **orientation conditioning**, but is not a guarantee that its **depth translation** improves monotonically. (pqac-00000013, pqac-00000014, pqac-00000030, pqac-00000048, pqac-00000049)

A separate HoloLens/ArUco evaluation found millimetre-scale, view- and distance-dependent *depth-axis biases*, demonstrating why tiny frame-to-frame variation is not evidence of accurate depth. But its marker was held perpendicular to the camera ray while sample locations moved from −30° to +30° in bearing; those results **cannot** be interpreted as a controlled comparison of frontal and tilted marker planes. At some extreme locations detection itself failed. (pqac-00000040, pqac-00000052)

## Recommendation for the proposed PiPER setup

1. **Keep the overhead camera for workspace clearance and policy context, but do not rely on it alone for fingertip height.** From the stated 102° × 67° field of view, an ideal camera pointed vertically down from **1.2 m** covers about **2.96 × 1.59 m** at table height—enough for the stated tabletop if its axes are suitably oriented and the table is centred. At the stated full resolution, that is roughly **0.64 mm per horizontal pixel** and **0.61 mm per vertical pixel** at the table plane; subpixel feature detection is possible, but these figures are *sampling pitches*, not calibrated 3D accuracy. Verify coverage at the **highest fingertip and arm positions**, where the footprint contracts, as well as at table height.

2. **Use the end-facing camera and a genuinely lateral room-side camera as the principal triangulating pair; also fuse the overhead view wherever the same fiducial is visible.** Aim for complementary, substantially separated rays through the *actual fingertip work volume*, rather than prescribing one universally optimal angle at the arm base. The proposed end camera’s **19° downward** aim and **0.42-m** height may yield a shallow sightline across the far tabletop and arm, while the low edge view may be blocked by objects or fingers. Test visibility and ray crossing at the near, far, high and low extremes before permanently mounting them. If the lateral camera cannot see the *same* feature as the end camera at those poses, move or raise it; three installed cameras can otherwise act like only one useful camera.

3. **Track a rigidly attached feature with a known transform to the fingertip tool-centre point (TCP).** A tag or ChArUco board supplies identified corners for cross-camera matching and calibration; a sphere avoids dependence on marker facing direction, but requires reliable centre detection and identity if multiple spheres are used. A rigid, multi-face or otherwise non-coplanar marker helps maintain identifiable corners as the wrist turns. Place the fiducial near the fingertips, characterize its mounting offset, and check that any orientation error does not become a large position error through that lever arm. LARK calibrated both camera extrinsics with a ChArUco board and the three-dimensional marker-corner geometry, then rejected inconsistent corner observations rather than trusting all views indiscriminately. (pqac-00000019, pqac-00000024, pqac-00000028, pqac-00000054)

4. **Validate the measurement system separately from the kinematics.** Calibrate each camera’s intrinsics and wide-lens distortion at its final focus and resolution; estimate inter-camera extrinsics with a measured board seen across the three-dimensional working volume, and securely mount cameras independently of the moving arm. Establish the board/table/robot-base transform and marker-to-TCP offset; then compare visually triangulated positions against encoder-based forward kinematics at *held-out poses spanning height and reach*. Report repeatability, systematic error and worst-case error separately, including fingertip poses with partial occlusion. To claim that a detected few-millimetre discrepancy is true robot drift, verify camera/TCP accuracy against an **independent** measured target or metrology reference—not merely the same robot commands used for calibration. Static image capture reduces blur and timing concerns; for motion, synchronize observations. (pqac-00000007, pqac-00000010, pqac-00000013, pqac-00000020, pqac-00000054)

**Bottom line:** the evidence supports **at least two well-calibrated cameras with complementary, appreciably separated sightlines**, and preferably a third for this cluttered, moving tabletop. It does **not** show that three cameras must always outperform two, that exactly 90° is optimal, or that one wide, overhead monocular image can independently verify few-millimetre *3D* fingertip drift. A single close camera with a well-designed **3D fiducial** can nevertheless provide useful relative pose measurements; that is a different, more marker- and calibration-dependent claim than robust multiview triangulation. (pqac-00000010, pqac-00000011, pqac-00000014, pqac-00000030)

The approach uses a single camera across multiple rigid manipulator poses and minimizes reprojection error jointly over those views, exploiting redundancy in the robot’s kinematics. contexts.context: LARK evaluated commodity RGB cameras with multiple viewpoints. Five cameras plus adaptive Kalman filtering achieved 1.13 mm point and 1.06 mm trajectory error on an anatomical phantom using triangulation, versus 1.35 and 1.53 mm for monocular pose fusion; on a machined grid, five-camera medians were 0.73 mm (monocular) and 0.85 mm (triangulation), compared with 0.69 mm fusionTrack. Triangulation stayed stable under poor views, while monocular fusion was vulnerable to outliers. A severely oblique, partially occluded single-marker view “compounds the tracking error.” Camera count and view quality both mattered.
contexts.question: Setup: a tabletop 6-DOF robot arm (AgileX PiPER, about 0.63 m reach, fingertips reach about 0.76 m at table height) on a 1.29 x 1.36 m table against a wall. We want fixed RGB cameras (Raspberry Pi Camera Module 3 Wide, 102 x 67 deg field of view, 4608 x 2592 px) that (a) triangulate the gripper fingertips to check the arm's joint-angle kinematics (detect drift of a few mm), (b) show whether the workspace is clear, and (c) may later feed learned visuomotor policies. Current proposal: one camera about 1.2 m above the table looking straight down, one about 0.8 m from the arm base past the table end the arm faces at joint 1 = 0, about 0.42 m up and tilted 19 deg down, and a third low camera on the room-side table edge looking toward the wall. For checking or calibrating the kinematic accuracy of a low-cost serial robot arm with fixed external cameras and a fiducial (ArUco, AprilTag or ChArUco board, or a sphere) on the end effector, what camera distances, viewing angles and numbers of cameras have given the best end-effector position accuracy, what accuracies (mm) were achieved, and how does the viewing angle of a planar fiducial (frontal vs oblique) affect its pose and depth accuracy? Does the evidence favour two or more cameras at large angular separation over a single camera?

contexts.context: The study tested fixed-camera fiducial tracking over 25 orientations (±30°) and 25 translations (±20 mm horizontal, ±40 mm depth), with ten images per pose. A single camera had a frontal-view near-mirror ambiguity: 2.18° orientation error (SD 0.80°) and 1.50 mm translation RMSE; errors improved when tilted ≥15°. Three multi-view “quARtet” layouts remained more consistent, achieving 0.24–0.47° frontal orientation error and 0.17–0.20 mm translation RMSE (within-cell SD 0.02–0.03 mm). Results are residuals after same-dataset frame alignment, not independent absolute calibration.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes camera-only pose estimation and multi-view triangulation, not camera-placement experiments or achieved millimetre accuracies. ArUco marker corners are detected, undistorted, and triangulated using calibrated intrinsics/extrinsics; each corner must be visible in at least two cameras. Reprojection errors above 8 pixels discard the marker, and corner weights equal the number of observing camera pairs, \(w_k=\frac12|\mathcal I_k|(|\mathcal I_k|-1)\). Measurements from \(n\) active cameras are stacked, giving \(6n\) observations, with covariance averaged across cameras. Thus it supports multiple-view triangulation but provides no evidence on distances, viewing angles, or frontal-versus-oblique planar-marker accuracy.

contexts.context: The cited results show strong dependence on geometry and tracking method. ArUco relative-pose errors were reported at camera distances of 500, 800, 1100, and 1400 mm; translation components varied from approximately −5.0 to +6.7 mm, with rotation errors up to 7.5°. contexts.context: The excerpt concerns fiducial tracking for AR, not robot-arm calibration specifically. It reports Frantz et al. testing hologram deviation at distances of **400–800 mm** and viewing angles from **−90° to +90°**, in **45° increments**, measuring xy error with graph paper and z error with a ruler. It also notes that marker size did not surprisingly guarantee better pose estimation at longer distances. Other cited work compared ArUco, 3D-model tracking, stereo cameras, retroreflective spheres, and OptiTrack, but the excerpt provides no numerical millimetre accuracies or direct comparison of one versus multiple cameras.
contexts.question: Setup: a tabletop 6-DOF robot arm (AgileX PiPER, about 0.63 m reach, fingertips reach about 0.76 m at table height) on a 1.29 x 1.36 m table against a wall. We want fixed RGB cameras (Raspberry Pi Camera Module 3 Wide, 102 x 67 deg field of view, 4608 x 2592 px) that (a) triangulate the gripper fingertips to check the arm's joint-angle kinematics (detect drift of a few mm), (b) show whether the workspace is clear, and (c) may later feed learned visuomotor policies. Current proposal: one camera about 1.2 m above the table looking straight down, one about 0.8 m from the arm base past the table end the arm faces at joint 1 = 0, about 0.42 m up and tilted 19 deg down, and a third low camera on the room-side table edge looking toward the wall. For checking or calibrating the kinematic accuracy of a low-cost serial robot arm with fixed external cameras and a fiducial (ArUco, AprilTag or ChArUco board, or a sphere) on the end effector, what camera distances, viewing angles and numbers of cameras have given the best end-effector position accuracy, what accuracies (mm) were achieved, and how does the viewing angle of a planar fiducial (frontal vs oblique) affect its pose and depth accuracy? Does the evidence favour two or more cameras at large angular separation over a single camera?

contexts.context: The excerpt provides the Wakiuchi et al. experimental setup for a single planar AprilTag control, but not the numerical results needed to determine whether a face-on 0° view produces the worst rotation, depth (z), or XY errors, nor whether a 15° angular threshold exists. Wakiuchi compared a 35 mm single planar tag36h11 marker with three 3D four-tag quARtet layouts. The single marker used one 35 mm tag, while experiments used a fixed Keyence camera observing a robot-mounted marker at an approximately 220 mm working distance. Pose was estimated with AprilTag detection and OpenCV solvePnP. The reference consisted of robot-commanded relative tilts and translations from an initial near-frontal pose, rather than independently calibrated ground truth; consequently, the excerpt cautions that sub-0.1 mm and orientation values are limited by protocol and reference uncertainty. No angle-by-angle error table, depth-axis error breakdown, distance sweep, or explicit distinction between camera/view-axis rotation and marker-plane tilt is included in the supplied pages. Costa 2024 is not mentioned in this excerpt, so its protocol and measured frontal-versus-oblique results cannot be established here. The text does distinguish commanded marker pose changes relative to the camera from absolute ground truth, but it does not report the requested numerical mm errors versus viewing angle.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes Costa et al. (2024)’s controlled Microsoft HoloLens 2 experiment using a single planar ArUco marker board, alongside ARToolkit and QR/Vuforia targets. The HoloLens PV camera was fixed, while the board was tested at five distances—300, 600, 900, 1200, and 1500 mm—and five orientations: −30°, −15°, 0°, +15°, and +30°. The board was kept perpendicular to the line joining each sampling point to the camera, and 500 consecutive pose observations were recorded at every point to estimate mean error and standard deviation. The excerpt states that translation error increased with distance for all trackers, independently of marker orientation. For ArUco specifically, significant problematic cases occurred at 300 mm with +30° and −30°; at such oblique angles the marker pattern could not always be detected correctly, and the collected samples included incorrect values. This supports a ±15°/±30° viewing-angle comparison, but the excerpt does not provide numerical millimetre errors by angle, separate depth-axis (Z) versus XY errors, rotation errors, or a comparison to ground truth. It also does not mention AprilTag or Wakiuchi’s single-tag experiment, nor distinguish camera/view-axis rotation from marker-plane tilt beyond the stated board-orientation protocol.

contexts.context: This excerpt supplies Costa et al.’s experimental structure and numerical pose-error data, but the explicitly identified table is for the QR Code tracker rather than AprilTag or ArUco. Measurements are reported at viewing angles of −15°, 0°, and +15° (with another preceding, unlabeled table also containing +30°), and at specified marker distances. For the QR tracker, the face-on 0° results are: at 300 mm, translation errors X/Y/Z = −3.07/0.83/4.20 mm; at 600 mm, −0.87/2.45/5.05 mm; and at 900 mm, 9.74/2.97/−33.86 mm. The −15° and +15° cases provide comparison values, including Z errors of 6.34 mm at 600 mm (−15°) and 3.00 mm at 900 mm (+15°). Rotation errors are given as θX, θY, and θZ in degrees, allowing view-axis rotation to be separated from translational/depth errors, although this excerpt does not define the coordinate convention, ground-truth protocol, marker-plane tilt interpretation, or a 15° angular threshold. Costa’s summary characterizes QR tracking as having accurate rotation estimation but limited resolution and working distance. No Wakiuchi protocol or explicit AprilTag-versus-ArUco frontal/oblique conclusion appears here.

contexts.context: The excerpt provides only a limited comparison relevant to frontal versus oblique planar AprilTag behavior. It explains that a single planar tag becomes geometrically ambiguous near a face-on view because perspective distortion weakens; small image errors can then produce large orientation changes, including flips between near-mirror pose solutions. It reports a single planar-tag baseline of 2.18° mean frontal orientation error and 1.50 mm root-mean-square position error, but does not provide a viewing-angle sweep, a 15° angular threshold, per-angle numerical errors, camera distance conditions, ground-truth values, or separate depth-axis (Z) and XY errors. The proposed quARtet marker improves the reported frontal errors, reaching 0.24–0.47° orientation error and 0.17–0.20 mm RMS position error, but these results concern the multi-tag layouts rather than a measured planar-tag angle-versus-error protocol. The excerpt also does not mention Costa 2024, ArUco experiments, or distinguish quantitatively between rotation about the viewing axis and marker-plane tilt. Thus, it can support the qualitative claim that near-frontal planar-tag orientation is least reliable, but it cannot supply the requested Costa protocol or detailed numerical comparison by viewing angle, distance, and ground truth.

contexts.context: This excerpt provides Costa et al.’s Hololens 2 planar-marker comparison, but it does not contain Wakiuchi’s single-planar-tag experiment or AprilTag results. Costa tested angular positions of -30°, -15°, 0°, 15°, and 30° and distances of 300–1500 mm. For example, at +30° and 1500 mm, translation errors were X = 14.49 ± 0.10 mm, Y = 2.11 ± 0.25 mm, and Z = -11.55 ± 0.51 mm. The excerpt does not state a 15° angular detection threshold; it only includes measurements at ±15°. It therefore supports angle-, distance-, and axis-specific comparison, but not direct ground-truth results for Wakiuchi or a dedicated frontal-versus-oblique AprilTag analysis.

contexts.context: The excerpt documents Wakiuchi et al.’s fixed-camera experiments for the single planar tag and three Quartet layouts, but it does not provide the requested Costa (2024) protocol or a complete angle-by-angle numerical table in the supplied pages. The broad orientation experiment used commanded tilts from −30° to +30° in 15° increments, with up to 10 consecutive frames per cell; the narrow experiment used −10° to +10° in 5° increments. Position commands covered ±20 mm horizontally and ±40 mm in depth, with depth represented by dy/Δz. Orientation error was computed as SO(3) geodesic angular distance between measured and robot-commanded relative rotations. Position translations were converted from meters to millimeters, with global axis-sign resolution and a 2D rigid Procrustes alignment before Euclidean residuals were calculated. Thus, the excerpt can support comparisons of frontal (θx=θy=0) versus oblique cells and identify depth-axis coverage, but it does not establish that 0° is worst or best, nor does it list numerical errors versus viewing angle or distance. Crucially, errors are relative to robot commands after same-dataset alignment—not independently calibrated ground truth. The protocol also distinguishes camera/view-axis rotation from marker-plane geometry: commanded orientation cells vary marker pose, while detector-side coordinates describe tilted tag planes and a marker frame whose +z faces the camera. The excerpt warns that fitted alignment removes constant marker-specific bias, so absolute pose accuracy cannot be inferred.

contexts.context: This excerpt describes the quARtet multi-tag marker rather than a measured comparison of a single planar AprilTag or ArUco marker at frontal versus oblique viewing angles. It provides no numerical millimetre errors for rotation, depth (z), or XY position, no results as a function of viewing angle or distance, no ground-truth comparison, and no explicit 15° angular threshold. The relevant conceptual point is that a single planar tag can suffer from near-frontal or near-mirror pose ambiguity; the excerpt states that this ambiguity can partially reappear when only one tilted tag remains visible. quARtet addresses this by tilting four tags and jointly solving one PnP problem from their shared 3D geometry. The implemented tilt is 18°, selected as a compromise between stronger non-frontal cues and a compact, fabrication-friendly form. The diagonal layout is described as improving off-axis visibility and reducing mutual occlusion, while pitch variants preserve graspable edges but may introduce geometric shadowing. The marker’s design tilt should not be confused with camera viewing-axis rotation: the passage discusses the physical tag-plane tilt and its effect on pose estimation, not a controlled experiment varying camera angle relative to a planar marker. Wakiuchi single-tag measurements and the Costa 2024 protocol are not included in this excerpt.

It states that the work empirically investigates “optimal” stereo-camera configurations to reduce spatial-discretization errors and develops a model estimating average triangulation error for convergent stereo. It emphasizes stereo calibration accuracy, uncertainty volumes, viewing-geometry trade-offs, and multiple-view geometry. contexts.question: Setup: a tabletop 6-DOF robot arm (AgileX PiPER, about 0.63 m reach, fingertips reach about 0.76 m at table height) on a 1.29 x 1.36 m table against a wall. We want fixed RGB cameras (Raspberry Pi Camera Module 3 Wide, 102 x 67 deg field of view, 4608 x 2592 px) that (a) triangulate the gripper fingertips to check the arm's joint-angle kinematics (detect drift of a few mm), (b) show whether the workspace is clear, and (c) may later feed learned visuomotor policies. Current proposal: one camera about 1.2 m above the table looking straight down, one about 0.8 m from the arm base past the table end the arm faces at joint 1 = 0, about 0.42 m up and tilted 19 deg down, and a third low camera on the room-side table edge looking toward the wall. For checking or calibrating the kinematic accuracy of a low-cost serial robot arm with fixed external cameras and a fiducial (ArUco, AprilTag or ChArUco board, or a sphere) on the end effector, what camera distances, viewing angles and numbers of cameras have given the best end-effector position accuracy, what accuracies (mm) were achieved, and how does the viewing angle of a planar fiducial (frontal vs oblique) affect its pose and depth accuracy? Does the evidence favour two or more cameras at large angular separation over a single camera?

contexts.context: The excerpt describes a multi-camera calibration approach using Raspberry Pi Global Shutter cameras (1456×1088, 60 fps) with 6 mm lenses, providing an approximately 837 mm horizontal field width at 1 m. Cameras are calibrated intrinsically with ChArUco boards across many poses and extrinsically through simultaneous board visibility, stereo calibration, and global bundle adjustment. ArUco markers are mounted on instruments; marker geometry is refined by bundle adjustment because coordinate errors directly degrade pose. Tracking uses triangulated corners and PnP, minimizing reprojection and 3D discrepancies across cameras.

answer.formatted_answer:
Question: Setup: a tabletop 6-DOF robot arm (AgileX PiPER, about 0.63 m reach, fingertips reach about 0.76 m at table height) on a 1.29 x 1.36 m table against a wall. We want fixed RGB cameras (Raspberry Pi Camera Module 3 Wide, 102 x 67 deg field of view, 4608 x 2592 px) that (a) triangulate the gripper fingertips to check the arm's joint-angle kinematics (detect drift of a few mm), (b) show whether the workspace is clear, and (c) may later feed learned visuomotor policies. Current proposal: one camera about 1.2 m above the table looking straight down, one about 0.8 m from the arm base past the table end the arm faces at joint 1 = 0, about 0.42 m up and tilted 19 deg down, and a third low camera on the room-side table edge looking toward the wall. For checking or calibrating the kinematic accuracy of a low-cost serial robot arm with fixed external cameras and a fiducial (ArUco, AprilTag or ChArUco board, or a sphere) on the end effector, what camera distances, viewing angles and numbers of cameras have given the best end-effector position accuracy, what accuracies (mm) were achieved, and how does the viewing angle of a planar fiducial (frontal vs oblique) affect its pose and depth accuracy? Does the evidence favour two or more cameras at large angular separation over a single camera?

## Evidence relevant to the camera layout

**Yes—two calibrated, substantially separated views are preferable to one for an independent three-dimensional check of the PiPER fingertips.** A third view is valuable primarily for surviving occlusion and improving coverage; it does not automatically improve precision. The studies below do not establish a universally optimal camera distance or crossing angle, nor do their best reported errors directly predict accuracy on this table. In particular, distinguish *camera-measurement error* from *robot error measured using cameras* and from *target-registration error after fitting a reference frame*. (sideris2026larkalowcost pages 12-13, sideris2026larkalowcost pages 13-14, wang2023separationandcalibration pages 21-23)

| Study and geometry / marker | Evaluation metric and measured accuracy | Interpretation |
|---|---|---|
| **Wang et al. (2023)** — binocular camera; ABB IRB-1200; three 25.4 mm ceramic spheres; camera-to-end-effector distance approximately 0.5–1.0 m (wang2023separationandcalibration pages 10-12, wang2023separationandcalibration pages 19-21) | Across 40 commanded motions of 50–100 mm: mean discrepancy **0.7873 to 0.2604 mm** after kinematic calibration; maximum **1.998 to 0.7107 mm** (wang2023separationandcalibration pages 21-23) | Strong short-range stereo result, but the camera measurement defines the observed motion; this is **not independently verified vision-localization error**. |
| **Wakiuchi et al. (2026)** — one fixed camera at approximately 0.22 m; 35 mm planar AprilTag versus 35 mm non-coplanar four-tag fiducials (wakiuchi2610quartetmarkera pages 10-12) | At fixed frontal orientation over a translation grid: planar-tag positional RMSE **1.50 mm**; non-coplanar four-tag designs **0.17–0.20 mm** (wakiuchi2610quartetmarkera pages 18-22) | Demonstrates near-frontal planar-tag ill-conditioning, not absolute accuracy: the reference was robot-commanded motion, and a constant transform was fitted to the evaluated data (wakiuchi2610quartetmarkera pages 42-44). |
| **Sideris et al. (2026), LARK — planar grid** — five Raspberry Pi global-shutter cameras in a pentagon on a 0.72 m fixture, approximately 1 m above the target; 24 mm ArUco tags on a dodecahedron (sideris2026larkalowcost pages 3-4, sideris2026larkalowcost pages 4-5) | Adaptive-triangulation **target-registration RMSE median**: 2 cameras **0.9584 mm**, 3 **1.0000 mm**, 4 **0.9030 mm**, 5 **0.7477 mm**. With five cameras, the median individual point error was **0.64 mm** (sideris2026larkalowcost pages 12-13, sideris2026larkalowcost pages 13-14). | Five cameras achieved submillimetre grid performance, but improvement with camera count was not monotonic: configuration and ray geometry mattered. The 0.7477 and 0.64 mm values summarize different units—trial/configuration RMSEs and individual target-point errors, respectively. |
| **Sideris et al. (2026), LARK — head phantom** — same hardware under greater depth variation, oblique views, and partial occlusion | One-camera monocular target-registration RMSE median **2.7304 mm**; adaptive triangulation: 2 cameras **1.7163 mm**, 3 **1.6082 mm**, 4 **1.3957 mm**, 5 **1.2774 mm**. Five-camera median individual point error: **1.13 mm** (sideris2026larkalowcost pages 12-13, sideris2026larkalowcost pages 14-17). | Accuracy improved consistently from two to five triangulating views, but realistic geometry eliminated the grid’s submillimetre result. Laboratory grid accuracy therefore should not be treated as whole-workspace absolute accuracy. |


*Table: Compact comparison of robot and fiducial localization results, including camera geometry, measured accuracy, and validation limitations. Values based on different aggregation methods are explicitly distinguished.*

The closest direct robot-calibration example is Wang and colleagues’ binocular measurement of three ceramic spheres on an ABB six-axis arm. At approximately **0.5–1.0 m** camera-to-end-effector distance, the mean discrepancy between commanded and vision-measured movements fell from **0.7873 to 0.2604 mm** after kinematic calibration; the post-calibration maximum was **0.7107 mm**. These are discrepancies *relative to the camera system*, not an independently established 0.26-mm accuracy for its sphere localization, and the industrial arm and optics differ from PiPER and Camera Module 3 Wide. (wang2023separationandcalibration pages 10-12, wang2023separationandcalibration pages 15-17, wang2023separationandcalibration pages 19-21, wang2023separationandcalibration pages 21-23)

For a controlled camera-count comparison, Sideris and colleagues placed **five** Raspberry Pi global-shutter cameras around a **72-cm-diameter** fixture approximately **1 m above** the measurement volume and tracked ArUco-marked three-dimensional fiducials. Their cropped Table 1 shows improving target-registration performance overall from one to five views, particularly on a three-dimensional phantom, but an intermediate three-camera triangulation configuration was *worse* than some two-camera configurations on the planar grid. Their approximately **0.64-mm** five-camera grid figure is a median *individual point* error; the corresponding **0.7477-mm** value in Table 1 is a median of trial/configuration RMSEs. Neither should be read as demonstrated fingertip accuracy across PiPER’s entire workspace. (sideris2026larkalowcost media 0630648e, sideris2026larkalowcost media 76d359f3, sideris2026larkalowcost media 54ca3ecb, sideris2026larkalowcost pages 3-4, sideris2026larkalowcost pages 9-10, sideris2026larkalowcost pages 12-13, sideris2026larkalowcost pages 13-14)

## Why viewing angles matter

There are **two different angles** to optimize. First, the *angle between rays from different cameras to the fingertip* should be substantial: nearly coincident cameras provide little independent depth information. For a conventional parallel stereo pair, depth uncertainty scales approximately as **Z²σd/(fB)**, where *Z* is range, *f* focal length in pixels, *B* baseline, and *σd* disparity uncertainty. This is a geometric approximation, **not** a measured error for the proposed cameras. A roughly orthogonal overhead–side pairing near the working region can therefore be useful, provided **both cameras actually see the same identifiable feature**. A wide baseline that loses joint visibility or produces severe marker foreshortening is counterproductive; LARK’s non-monotonic subset results illustrate that qualification. (sideris2026larkalowcost pages 10-12, sideris2026larkalowcost pages 12-13, sideris2026larkalowcost pages 13-14, sideris2026larkalowcost pages 8-9)

Second, consider the angle **between each camera’s sightline and a planar marker’s normal**. A nearly face-on tag can have excellent apparent area yet weak perspective cues for its *tilt*, permitting competing near-mirror pose estimates; an extremely oblique tag loses projected area and detectable corners. In a particularly relevant **single fixed-camera**, approximately **220-mm-range** experiment, a 35-mm planar AprilTag gave **2.18° ± 0.80°** frontal orientation error, versus approximately **0.15–0.6°** across oblique cells with commanded tilts of **15–30°**. Its positional RMSE over translations made *while held frontally* was **1.50 mm**, compared with **0.17–0.20 mm** for non-coplanar four-tag markers occupying the same footprint. Those position figures combine coordinate directions, including commanded depth changes: the study does **not** establish a separate 1.50-mm depth error. Crucially, its reference was robot-commanded *relative* motion with an alignment fitted on the evaluated measurements—not external absolute ground truth. Moderate obliquity helps the planar tag’s **orientation conditioning**, but is not a guarantee that its **depth translation** improves monotonically. (wakiuchi2610quartetmarkera pages 12-18, wakiuchi2610quartetmarkera pages 18-22, wakiuchi2610quartetmarkera pages 10-12, wakiuchi2610quartetmarkera pages 36-42, wakiuchi2610quartetmarkera pages 42-44)

A separate HoloLens/ArUco evaluation found millimetre-scale, view- and distance-dependent *depth-axis biases*, demonstrating why tiny frame-to-frame variation is not evidence of accurate depth. But its marker was held perpendicular to the camera ray while sample locations moved from −30° to +30° in bearing; those results **cannot** be interpreted as a controlled comparison of frontal and tilted marker planes. At some extreme locations detection itself failed. (costa2024assessmentofmultiple pages 9-10, costa2024assessmentofmultiple pages 15-17)

## Recommendation for the proposed PiPER setup

1. **Keep the overhead camera for workspace clearance and policy context, but do not rely on it alone for fingertip height.** From the stated 102° × 67° field of view, an ideal camera pointed vertically down from **1.2 m** covers about **2.96 × 1.59 m** at table height—enough for the stated tabletop if its axes are suitably oriented and the table is centred. At the stated full resolution, that is roughly **0.64 mm per horizontal pixel** and **0.61 mm per vertical pixel** at the table plane; subpixel feature detection is possible, but these figures are *sampling pitches*, not calibrated 3D accuracy. Verify coverage at the **highest fingertip and arm positions**, where the footprint contracts, as well as at table height.

2. **Use the end-facing camera and a genuinely lateral room-side camera as the principal triangulating pair; also fuse the overhead view wherever the same fiducial is visible.** Aim for complementary, substantially separated rays through the *actual fingertip work volume*, rather than prescribing one universally optimal angle at the arm base. The proposed end camera’s **19° downward** aim and **0.42-m** height may yield a shallow sightline across the far tabletop and arm, while the low edge view may be blocked by objects or fingers. Test visibility and ray crossing at the near, far, high and low extremes before permanently mounting them. If the lateral camera cannot see the *same* feature as the end camera at those poses, move or raise it; three installed cameras can otherwise act like only one useful camera.

3. **Track a rigidly attached feature with a known transform to the fingertip tool-centre point (TCP).** A tag or ChArUco board supplies identified corners for cross-camera matching and calibration; a sphere avoids dependence on marker facing direction, but requires reliable centre detection and identity if multiple spheres are used. A rigid, multi-face or otherwise non-coplanar marker helps maintain identifiable corners as the wrist turns. Place the fiducial near the fingertips, characterize its mounting offset, and check that any orientation error does not become a large position error through that lever arm. LARK calibrated both camera extrinsics with a ChArUco board and the three-dimensional marker-corner geometry, then rejected inconsistent corner observations rather than trusting all views indiscriminately. (sideris2026larkalowcost pages 3-4, wang2023separationandcalibration pages 10-12, sideris2026larkalowcost pages 8-9, sideris2026larkalowcost pages 4-5)

4. **Validate the measurement system separately from the kinematics.** Calibrate each camera’s intrinsics and wide-lens distortion at its final focus and resolution; estimate inter-camera extrinsics with a measured board seen across the three-dimensional working volume, and securely mount cameras independently of the moving arm. Establish the board/table/robot-base transform and marker-to-TCP offset; then compare visually triangulated positions against encoder-based forward kinematics at *held-out poses spanning height and reach*. Report repeatability, systematic error and worst-case error separately, including fingertip poses with partial occlusion. To claim that a detected few-millimetre discrepancy is true robot drift, verify camera/TCP accuracy against an **independent** measured target or metrology reference—not merely the same robot commands used for calibration. Static image capture reduces blur and timing concerns; for motion, synchronize observations. (sideris2026larkalowcost pages 5-7, sideris2026larkalowcost pages 12-13, wakiuchi2610quartetmarkera pages 12-18, maghami2024visionbasedtargetlocalization pages 14-17, sideris2026larkalowcost pages 4-5)

**Bottom line:** the evidence supports **at least two well-calibrated cameras with complementary, appreciably separated sightlines**, and preferably a third for this cluttered, moving tabletop. It does **not** show that three cameras must always outperform two, that exactly 90° is optimal, or that one wide, overhead monocular image can independently verify few-millimetre *3D* fingertip drift. A single close camera with a well-designed **3D fiducial** can nevertheless provide useful relative pose measurements; that is a different, more marker- and calibration-dependent claim than robust multiview triangulation. (sideris2026larkalowcost pages 12-13, sideris2026larkalowcost pages 13-14, wakiuchi2610quartetmarkera pages 18-22, wakiuchi2610quartetmarkera pages 10-12)

info.query: Setup: a tabletop 6-DOF robot arm (AgileX PiPER, about 0.63 m reach, fingertips reach about 0.76 m at table height) on a 1.29 x 1.36 m table against a wall. We want fixed RGB cameras (Raspberry Pi Camera Module 3 Wide, 102 x 67 deg field of view, 4608 x 2592 px) that (a) triangulate the gripper fingertips to check the arm's joint-angle kinematics (detect drift of a few mm), (b) show whether the workspace is clear, and (c) may later feed learned visuomotor policies. Current proposal: one camera about 1.2 m above the table looking straight down, one about 0.8 m from the arm base past the table end the arm faces at joint 1 = 0, about 0.42 m up and tilted 19 deg down, and a third low camera on the room-side table edge looking toward the wall. For checking or calibrating the kinematic accuracy of a low-cost serial robot arm with fixed external cameras and a fiducial (ArUco, AprilTag or ChArUco board, or a sphere) on the end effector, what camera distances, viewing angles and numbers of cameras have given the best end-effector position accuracy, what accuracies (mm) were achieved, and how does the viewing angle of a planar fiducial (frontal vs oblique) affect its pose and depth accuracy? Does the evidence favour two or more cameras at large angular separation over a single camera?
